Industry News: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 70 min read (13910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~70 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2.
  • Transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12.
  • In a recent development, the inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3,4,5,6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) reveals the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

Transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12. CASTs have evolved repeatedly by exaptation of minimal, nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas systems to enable RNA-guided, site-specific DNA integration13,14,15. These systems operate through the concerted action of a CRISPR-based targeting module and a Tn7-like transposition machinery comprising the TnsC AAA+ ATPase, the TnsB transposase and, in some systems, the TnsA endonuclease. The CASTs characterized so far differ mainly in the organization of their DNA-targeting and transposition modules1,2,16,17,18. Type I variants typically use a multi-subunit Cascade–TniQ (QCascade) complex for target recognition guided by CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and TnsA–TnsB for cut-and-paste transposition19,20,21. By contrast, type V-K systems rely on the Cas12k–TniQ–S15 complex for crRNA-guided targeting5 and use only TnsB for copy-and-paste transposition, resulting in cointegrate products22. TnsC plays a pivotal part in all CASTs, acting as an adapter that bridges the targeting module and the transposase enzymes to define the insertion site23,24.

In a recent development, the inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA. CAST-based editing has been implemented in bacteria25,26,27,28 and mammalian cells7,8,29,30, offering considerable potential for research and therapeutic applications. Type V-K CASTs generally show low integration efficiencies in human cell lines29,30, limited specificity2,26,27,31 and heterogeneous insertion profiles22,30. By contrast, type I-F systems can perform precise, simple insertions with substantially higher efficiencies1,7,22,26. In particular, the type I-F system of the Pseudoalteromonas Tn7016 transposon (Fig. 1a) has emerged as a highly promising candidate for genome-engineering applications, because of its uniquely high integration activity in human cells7,9. Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering of PseCAST components in Escherichia coli have resulted in the evoCAST system. This system has markedly improved integration efficiencies, reaching up to 10–30% in human cells, yet maintains precise, cointegrate-free insertion outcomes8. Although structural studies of type V-K CAST systems have provided mechanistic insights into various stages of transpososome assembly5,6,32,33,34,35,36, structural information about type I CASTs is presently limited to sub-complexes9,19,20,21,37,38,39,40,41,42. This presents a knowledge gap in the mechanistic understanding of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway. Specifically, the mechanism by which the RNA-guided targeting module induces the assembly and catalytic activation of the transposase components remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that a, Locus organization of the type I-F CAST of Pseudoalteromonas sp. S983 (Tn7016). RE, right transposon end; LE, left transposon end. b, Cryo-EM density map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC targeting complex bound to DNA, coloured as in a. c, Atomic model of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, coloured as in b. d, Schematic of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, highlighting individual subunits. e, DNA organization in the targeting complex (left), with an accompanying diagram summarizing strand identity and protein footprints derived from the model (right). TGS, target strand; NTGS, non-target strand. f–h, Magnifications of the interactions between TniQ.1, TnsC.1 and TnsC.7, highlighting hydrophobic (f) and ionic (g) contacts as well as bridging interactions of TniQ.1 with the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (h). i, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TniQ–TnsC interface, as determined by quantitative PCR (qPCR). j–l, Magnifications of the interaction interface between Cas8 and TnsC.5, highlighting electrostatic (j), polar (k) and aromatic (l) contacts. m, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST with mutations in the Cas8–TnsC interface, as determined by qPCR. i,m, Data are mean ± s.d. of three independent biological replicates (n = 3; circles); the catalytically inactive mutant TnsB(D220A) serves as a negative control.

It has been revealed that here we report a series of structural snapshots of the PseCAST system obtained using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a previously unresolved transpososome holocomplex assembly comprising all molecular components. These snapshots reveal the molecular determinants and critical checkpoints at key stages of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway, including target DNA recognition, TnsC oligomerization, transposase recruitment and catalytic activation. Our findings define the molecular mechanisms that govern RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs, thereby establishing a structural foundation for the further development of these systems as genome-engineering tools.

TnsC oligomers function as bridging modules for the assembly of the transposition machinery in both type V-K and type I-B CASTs, interacting with the RNA-guided CRISPR module through their amino-terminal face and with the transposase through their carboxy-terminal face6,20,36,41. To elucidate the structural basis of the guide-RNA-dependent assembly of TnsC in the type I-F PseCAST, our initial cryo-EM analysis yielded a reconstruction of a target-DNA-bound complex comprising PseCascade–TniQ and a heptameric TnsC ring (hereafter the targeting complex) at an overall resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 1b–d, Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Resembling the architecture of TnsC heptamers from the canonical Tn7 element of E. coli and other type I CAST systems20,40,42,43 (Extended Data Fig. 2), the TnsC heptamer has a near-perfect seven-fold symmetry without a helical rise or seam, fully enclosing the DNA duplex in a positively charged central channel, in which all seven TnsC ATPase sites are occupied by ATP molecules and Mg2+ ions. The enclosed DNA adopts B-form geometry and is contacted by the Glu105–Asp120 loops of TnsC.1 and TnsC.5 through nonspecific interactions.

Notably, the structure of the targeting complex includes a complete 32-base-pair R-loop (Fig. 1e), which was only partially formed in the previously reported intermediate PseQCascade complex structure9. In contrast to the open arrangement of the partial R-loop intermediate9, the Cas8 α-helical bundle (residues 272–421) undergoes an approximately 90° rotation into a closed or locked state (Extended Data Fig. 3a), establishing additional contacts with the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM)-distal segment of the target DNA, both TniQ subunits and Cas7.5 (Extended Data Fig. 3b–d). Moreover, three nucleotides of the displaced non-target strand (NTGS) are bound in a pocket in the Cas8 bundle (Extended Data Fig. 3e), which likely facilitates reannealing of the NTGS with the target strand (TGS) in the PAM-distal DNA segment and its interactions with the TniQ dimer. This feature is absent from the partial R-loop and open helical-bundle states of type I-F CAST QCascade complexes published previously19,21. As the presence of a full R-loop and a closed Cas8 helical-bundle conformation have been suggested to be a prerequisite for stable target engagement21, our structural observations indicate that the formation of the locked state serves as a target fidelity checkpoint upstream of transposase recruitment.

Unexpectedly, the structure of the PseCAST targeting complex revealed that the TnsC heptamer interacts with both TniQ.1 and Cas8 through extensive interfaces spanning 947 Å2 and 818 Å2, respectively (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 3f), forming a ‘super-ring’ assembly that bridges the PAM-proximal and PAM-distal ends of the QCascade subcomplex. At the N-terminal face of the heptamer, TnsC protomers use the same surfaces for interactions with both TniQ and Cas8 (Extended Data Fig. 3f). At the PAM-distal end, the N-terminal region of TniQ.1 is wedged into the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 inter-subunit interface. An aromatic pocket in TniQ.1 comprising Phe3, Phe5, Phe29 and Phe30 interacts with a hydrophobic loop in TnsC.1 containing Leu101, Leu104, Leu106, Phe107 and Ile112 (Fig. 1f). TnsC.1 further engages TniQ.1 in a series of ionic interactions (Fig. 1g) and bridging interactions that also contact the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (Fig. 1h). Individual mutations in the inserted TnsC loop (L106S or F107A) did not affect the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. By contrast, a strong synergistic effect in the TnsC double mutant L106A, F107A led to a near-complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Whereas alanine substitutions in pairs of residues in the TniQ hydrophobic pocket (either F3A and F5A, or F29A and F30A) had a mild effect on transposition efficiency (Fig. 1i), charge-reversal substitutions at these positions (either F3E and F5E, or F29E and F30E) had a substantially stronger effect (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Deletion of the seven N-terminal TniQ residues resulted in the loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Moreover, cross-subunit mutant combinations involving residues in the TnsC loop and the TniQ hydrophobic pocket, either TnsC(L106S) and TniQ(F3A, F5A), or TnsC(F107A) and TniQ(F29A, F30A), resulted in a marked decrease in or the complete loss of transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1i), confirming the importance of the TniQ–TnsC interactions for the assembly of the PseCAST transpososome.

At the PAM-proximal end, Cas8 and TnsC.5 form a shape-complementary interface, mediated by aromatic and electrostatic interactions (Fig. 1j–l). The combination of TnsC mutations R68A, Y75A, R77A and Pheresulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1m), indicating that the Cas8–TnsC interaction contributes to transpososome assembly. However, mutations of interacting residues in Cas8, alone or in cross-subunit combinations with TnsC, had a mild or negligible effect (Fig. 1m), suggesting that the sensitivity of the TnsC–Cas8 interface to mutational perturbations is lower than that of the TnsC–TniQ interface. Similarly, whereas the individual charge-reversal TnsC mutant Y75E alone was sufficient to decrease transposition activity substantially, single charge-reversal mutations in Cas8 (T486R, W465E or H469E) had variable effects on transposition efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Together, these structural observations define the molecular coupling between the CRISPR targeting machinery and TnsC that results in the assembly of an ATP-loaded TnsC heptamer on the target DNA.

In the canonical Tn7 element in E. coli44, as well as in the type V-K CAST system of Scytonema hofmanni (ShCAST) and the type I-B CAST system of Peltigera membranacea cyanobiont 210A (PmcCAST), transposase recruitment is mediated by TnsC interactions with the C-terminal region of TnsB6,23,41. In the structure of the paired-end complex (PEC) of PseTnsAB, the C-terminal tail of PseTnsB (residues 574–613) is disordered45. To assess whether the unstructured tail plays a similar part in interacting with PseTnsC, we performed co-precipitation experiments using affinity-tagged PseTnsB constructs comprising either the full-length protein or the standalone C-terminal tail (TnsB(575–613)) (Fig. 2a). Both full-length TnsB and TnsB(575–613) co-precipitated target-DNA-bound QCascade and TnsC efficiently in the presence of ATP (Fig. 2b), indicating that TnsB interacts directly with the targeting complex and that its C-terminal tail is sufficient for this interaction. The amount of co-precipitated TnsC remained unchanged in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue ATPγS (Extended Data Fig. 4a), indicating that, similar to the type I-B PmcCAST system41,42, TnsB does not stimulate ATPase-dependent depolymerization of TnsC in PseCAST. Furthermore, co-precipitation of TnsC by TnsB(575–613) decreased strongly in the absence of ATP, suggesting that the interaction requires ATP-dependent TnsC oligomerization (Extended Data Fig. 4b). This result was corroborated by the loss of TnsC co-precipitation in the absence of QCascade or after introducing mutations in the TniQ- and Cas8-interacting interfaces (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Together, these results indicate that TnsB recruitment requires QCascade-dependent assembly of TnsC on the target DNA.

According to recent reports, a, Domain organization of PseTnsA, PseTnsB and an artificial PseTnsAB fusion protein. Numbers above the schematic refer to amino-acid positions for individual proteins; numbers below refer to the PseTnsAB fusion protein. CAT, catalytic domain; C-tail, C-terminal tail; DBD1 and DBD2, DNA-binding domains 1 and 2, respectively; NLS, nuclear localization signal. The C-terminal hook motif (residues 605–613) is highlighted in yellow. b, Co-precipitation of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC targeting complex by amylose-immobilized His6–MBP-tagged full-length TnsB (left) or C-terminal tail (right) in the presence of ATP and target DNA. CQC, Cascade–TniQ–TnsC; I, 5% input control; E, elution. Representative results from two independent replicates are shown. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 2. c, Cryo-EM density map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC transposase recruitment complex bound to TnsB hook motifs. d, Atomic model of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC transposase recruitment complex bound to TnsB hook motifs. The seventh TnsB hook is located at the back of the structure and is not visible in this side view. e, Right, atomic model of the TnsB hook-decorated TnsC heptamer. Left, magnification of the interactions between TnsC.2 and the TnsB.2 hook motif. f, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TnsB hook, as determined by qPCR. Data are mean ± s.d. of three independent biological replicates (n = 3; circles); TnsB mutation D220A serves as a negative control.

To validate these findings structurally, we aimed to reconstitute and determine the structure of QCascade–TnsC in complex with TnsAB bound to the excised transposon ends. To this end, we performed affinity co-precipitation using a recombinant TnsAB fusion protein construct (Fig. 2a), pre-assembled with a segment of the right end of the transposon (RE), to capture the QCascade–TnsC complex assembled on the target substrate comprising a linear double-stranded DNA (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Single-particle cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample yielded a 2.8-Å reconstruction of a PseCAST transposase recruitment complex comprising target-bound QCascade and heptamerized TnsC decorated with TnsB C-terminal segments (or TnsB hooks; residues Trp605–Glu613). The TnsB hooks are bound to all TnsC subunits at the junction between the N-terminal α/β core domain and the C-terminal α-helical bundle close to the ATP binding pocket (Fig. 2c,d, Extended Data Table 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c), similar to the arrangement described for type V-K34,36 and I-B41,42 CASTs (Extended Data Fig. 6). They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions of TnsB residues Trp605, Leu609 and Phe612 and an additional hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of residue Asp606 of TnsB and Arg212 of TnsC (Fig. 2e). Corroborating these observations, TnsB mutation W605A caused a substantial decrease in the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. Moreover, individual TnsB mutations L609K or F612A, as well as the deletion of the entire TnsB hook (Δ604–613) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 2f). These findings highlight the functional requirement of the interactions between the TnsB hook and TnsC for the transposition activity of PseCAST and demonstrate the critical role of the TnsB C-terminal tail in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase and for the delivery of the transposon DNA to the target site before integration.

Industry observers note that to determine the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex comprising Cascade, TniQ, TnsC and TnsAB, we used a modified ‘one pot’ affinity co-precipitation strategy to trap the transpososome in a post-integration strand-transfer complex (STC) state (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7), which has been used previously to visualize transpososome structures because of its stability6,34,36,41,46,47. The assembly used a minimal symmetrized RE donor sequence, which supports transposition in related systems48,49 and is sufficient for the formation of a paired-end PseTnsAB complex45. Cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample, supported by three-dimensional variability analysis combined with heterogeneous and locally focused refinement, yielded a reconstruction with a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Table 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). The reconstruction revealed that the transposase adopts an intertwined, pseudo-twofold arrangement with a TnsA2–TnsB4 stoichiometry to assemble on the structured DNA in an STC configuration (Fig. 3c,d). All seven TnsC subunits are bound to the C-terminal hook motifs of TnsAB (Fig. 3b,c); it is not possible to ascertain which of these are connected to the bound TnsAB or contributed by unbound TnsAB molecules in trans, as the connecting segments (residues 824–843) of TnsAB are unstructured. The target DNA exits from the central channel of the TnsC heptamer and extends towards the TnsAB tetramer assembled on the pseudo-palindromic target site duplication (TSD) region and the adjacent transposon end sequences (Fig. 3a). As in the structure of the TnsAB PEC45, each transposon end is occupied by two TnsB protomers: a proximal catalytic subunit (TnsB.1 or TnsB.2)—the catalytic domain of which engages the other transposon end in trans—and a distal structural subunit (TnsB.3 or TnsB.4) (Fig. 3c). Only two TnsA subunits (TnsA.1 and TnsA.2), bound to the catalytic TnsB protomers, are resolved in the structure. The corresponding interaction interfaces in the structural TnsB subunits are occupied by the bound RE DNA duplexes, precluding TnsA interactions.

Sources indicate that the structure of the PseCAST holocomplex reveals the molecular interactions responsible for the TnsC-dependent recruitment of TnsAB to the target DNA to effect site-specific donor integration. The TnsB.1 subunit is tethered to the C-terminal face of the TnsC heptamer by its β-barrel domain (residues 434–500), positioned at the interface of the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits (Fig. 3e). TnsC.1 inserts its C-terminal loop—spanning residues 314–322 and including Leu318—into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Val472, Gln467 and Leu441 in the TnsB.1 β-barrel domain (Fig. 3e). In turn, Asn316 of TnsC, situated in the same loop in TnsC.7, interacts through hydrogen bonds with Arg443 and Asn444 in TnsB.1 (Fig. 3e). Aspartate substitutions of Leu318 in TnsC (L318D) or Val472 in TnsB (V472D) resulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 3f). The single TnsC mutation N316A or replacement of TnsC loop residues 316–321 with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker resulted in modestly impaired activity. By contrast, the single TnsB mutations R443E or N444D strongly reduced transposition activity (Fig. 3f), confirming that the formation of this interface is essential for PseCAST-mediated DNA transposition.

According to recent reports, in addition to interactions with TnsC, the β-barrel domain of the catalytic TnsB.1 subunit also interacts with the backbone of the target DNA segment downstream of the TnsC heptamer, forming a network of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic contacts using Arg439, Thr440, Lys447 and Gln449 of TnsB (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, Lys520 and Arg524 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB also contact the target DNA backbone. Notably, this domain adopts a helical bundle fold that bridges the catalytic and β-barrel domains in the catalytic TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits. By contrast, the helical domain of the structural TnsB.3 and TnsB.4 subunits forms two stretched helices that are sandwiched between the catalytic domain and DNA-binding domain 2 of TnsAB.1 and TnsAB.2, contributing to intra-subunit contacts.

It has been revealed that together, these insights highlight the functional role of the TnsB β-barrel domain in transpososome assembly. The shape complementarity of the TnsC and TnsB β-barrel interaction surfaces, together with cooperative interactions with the target DNA, provide the structural basis for the molecular ruler mechanism that defines the integration site, enabling the transposon to be inserted at a fixed distance of 49 nucleotides from the crRNA-specified target site. Moreover, the synergistic contacts with two TnsC subunits and the target DNA underlie a checkpoint mechanism that senses target DNA-dependent TnsC oligomerization, thereby explaining the strictly sequential assembly of the transpososome observed in type I-F systems40.

It has been revealed that the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex captures the TnsAB STC tetramer in a post-integration state (Fig. 4a,b). As in the PEC structure45, the active sites of the TnsA.1 and TnsA.2 subunits interact with the 5′ termini of the transposon ends, adopting a catalytically competent, post-cleavage geometry in which the catalytic triad residues Glu34, Asp71 and Lys87 of TnsA coordinate the 5′-terminal phosphate group and a single Mg2+ ion (Fig. 4c). In contrast to the PEC structure, the catalytic sites of the TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits also assume an activated conformation in which a Mg2+ ion—coordinated by the catalytic triad residues Asp220, Asp304 and Glu340 of TnsB—interacts with the 3′-hydroxyl group of the terminal nucleotide (dG76 in the NTGS) of the target DNA and the phosphodiester group that links the TSD segment to the 3′-terminal nucleotide of the transposon end (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, the catalytic domain establishes contacts with RE and TSD nucleotides that are crucial for STC formation (Fig. 4d). Specifically, Asp225 of TnsB positions an additional Mg2+ ion such that it simultaneously coordinates the phosphate groups of dA(−82) and dG(−80), stabilizing a kink in the DNA backbone at the TSD–RE junction that enables STC formation. The backbone is additionally contacted by Thr222, Arg239 and Ser360 of TnsB (Fig. 4d). Consistent with these observations, alanine substitution of Asp225 (D225A) or a charge-reversal mutation of Arg239 of TnsB (R239E) resulted in a complete loss of PseCAST transposition activity in E. coli, whereas TnsB mutations T222A or S360A only reduced PseCAST activity (Fig. 4e).

TnsB domains that become structured in the STC are indicated. c, Magnification of the 5′-terminal transposon-end overhang in the catalytic site of TnsA. d, Magnification of the TnsB catalytic site and interactions between the TSD DNA and the TnsB catalytic domain. e, RNA-guided transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST systems containing mutations in the TnsB residues involved in contacting the TSD region of the target DNA, as quantified by qPCR. f, Magnification of the interface between the β-barrel, C-terminal helical domain, C-terminal tail and catalytic domains of TnsB in the STC. g,h, Magnifications of the structural overlays of TnsAB in the PEC (blue) and STC (orange) states. g, Allosteric remodelling of the TnsB catalytic domain, ordering of the region comprising TnsB residues 346–369 and shift in the helix containing the catalytic residue Glu340 of TnsB. h, Ordering of the first 12 N-terminal residues of TnsA. i, RNA-guided transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST systems containing mutations in the N-terminus of TnsA and in the residues at the interface shown in f, as quantified by qPCR. e,i, Data are mean ± s.d. of three biologically independent replicates (n = 3; circles); TnsB mutation D220A serves as a negative control.

Finally, the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex structure highlights a potential allosteric relay mechanism that underlies the target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB. In the PEC structure, the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the catalytic TnsB subunits are disordered45. By contrast, both domains are structured in the STC state and interface with the catalytic domain (Fig. 4b) through a network of hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions (Fig. 4f). This is coupled with local structural remodelling of the catalytic domain, resulting in the ordering of an adjacent loop (residues Glu348–Lys369 of TnsB) (Fig. 4g) and an approximately 11-Å concomitant shift of the helix bearing the catalytic Glu340 residue of TnsB (Fig. 4g). The conformational rearrangement marks the transition of the catalytic site from an inactive, post-excision state to an active, strand-transfer configuration that supports Mg2+ coordination and catalytic activity. Consistent with these observations, combined alanine substitutions of Lys567, Gln571 and Asn577 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB strongly reduced the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli (Fig. 4i). Additional ordering was observed for the N-terminal segment (residues Met1–Pro11) of the TnsA helical domain, which positions the Arg4 residue of TnsA such that it contacts the 5′-terminal phosphate of the cleaved transposon end (Fig. 4c,h), implicating TnsA in TnsB activation. Accordingly, truncation of the TnsA N-terminal segment (ΔMet1–Asn12) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 4i). Together, the structural observations and their functional validation indicate that the molecular interfaces formed between the C-terminal, β-barrel and catalytic domains of TnsB after binding to the target DNA and TnsC are required to support the integration activity of PseCAST. Both target DNA and TnsC synergistically couple transposase recruitment with domain ordering and catalytic-site remodelling, resulting in the allosteric activation of TnsB for site-specific DNA integration.

According to recent reports, our structural and functional analyses of the PseCAST system comprehensively revealed the molecular mechanism that underlies RNA-guided transposon integration by type I-F CASTs, in which an orchestrated series of interactions and conformational rearrangements couples target recognition with site-specific DNA insertion. Together, these insights support a mechanistic model in which DNA transposition is controlled by a succession of molecular checkpoints (Fig. 5). The formation of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex requires R-loop completion, enabled by a conformational rearrangement of the Cas8 subunit, including the approximately 90° rotation of the helical bundle domain into a locked conformation. In contrast to the open conformations reported previously for type I-F CAST QCascade complexes9,19,21,37, this locked state positions the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex for binding to TniQ, which facilitates ATP-dependent TnsC assembly on the target DNA by interacting with Cas8 and TniQ. As the locked Cas8 conformation is achieved only with fully matched targets, it acts as a fidelity checkpoint that discriminates against mismatched sites, underpinning the high target specificity of PseCAST. Instead of forming extended filaments as in type V CASTs32,33, PseTnsC assembles into a symmetric heptamer to fully encircle the DNA duplex exiting QCascade. The transposon insertion site is thus defined by the physical footprint and register of the TnsC ring, rather than by TnsB-dependent TnsC depolymerization6,32,33. The initial recruitment of the TnsAB transposase PEC is mediated by the TnsB C-terminal tail hook motifs. As these interactions are dependent on TnsC heptamerization, this step provides another fidelity checkpoint that makes transposition dependent on the correct recognition of the DNA target. Finally, productive target engagement by TnsAB requires conformational ordering of the TnsB β-barrel domain and C-terminal helices, driven by interactions of the TnsB β-barrel domain with the target DNA and the TnsC heptamer. This is coupled with structural remodelling of the TnsB active site into a catalytically competent configuration. Therefore, the TnsC- and target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB acts as a final fidelity checkpoint, ensuring that transposon DNA insertion proceeds only once the transposase is correctly anchored to the target DNA. Together, our findings reveal the structural coupling of target DNA engagement and transposase activation, but the precise role of allosteric interactions in the observed conformational rearrangements requires further investigation. We speculate that similar structural coupling is involved in activating TnsAB for transposon excision after interacting with the flanking segments of the donor DNA.

It has been revealed that the Cascade–TniQ complex is guided to the target DNA by base-pairing with its crRNA, leading to the initial formation of a partial R-loop. Coordination of the displaced NTGS by the Cas8 helical bundle is coupled with the transition of the bundle from open to closed, full R-loop formation and the stabilization of the double-stranded PAM-distal target-DNA duplex by the TniQ dimer. TnsC is recruited to the target site, where it assembles into a closed heptameric ring by binding to the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex in the presence of ATP, TniQ and Cas8. At the donor site, excision of the transposon DNA by TnsAB involves the formation of a PEC. The PEC is initially recruited by the TnsC heptamer by interacting with the C-terminal TnsB hooks. Interactions with the target DNA and TnsC result in structural remodelling of the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the interfacing TnsB copies, which is allosterically coupled with a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic domains into an active conformation (the asterisks indicate active TnsB sites). The transposon DNA is integrated by two transesterification reactions catalysed by the active sites of the interfacing TnsBs, covalently linking both transposon 3′ ends to the target DNA with 5-base-pair spacing that results in a target-site duplication (TSD).

Sources indicate that directed evolution and structure-guided engineering are powerful complementary strategies for improving CAST activity8,9, recalling previous studies in which structural insights have enabled the rational design of hyperactive variants of the Sleeping Beauty transposase50,51. To provide a structural context for current engineering efforts, we mapped the activity-enhancing substitutions of evoCAST onto the PseCAST holocomplex structure (Extended Data Fig. 9). Two of these, F43S in TnsB and P88T in TnsA, have already been interpreted structurally in the PseTnsAB PEC as potentially facilitating transposon end recognition and stabilizing the cleaved NTGS overhang, respectively. Several of the remaining substitutions in TnsB, which were mostly unresolved in the PEC, can now be interpreted. Y349N, P352T and D396N are found close to the target-DNA substrate, potentially enhancing its binding. Q410K, V526E and Q549R are predominantly surface-facing and thus likely to enhance protein solubility or stability. Q594L, although unresolved in the holocomplex structure, may provide additional hydrophobic interactions to the interface formed between the C-terminal hook and TnsC, which is essential for transposase recruitment. Finally, H464R may promote the interaction between the TnsB β-barrel domain and TnsC through enhanced electrostatic contacts. The substitutions R197I and N314K in TnsC map to the TnsC oligomerization interface and the TnsC–TnsB interface, respectively. Lastly, in addition to the PAM-enhancing mutations N125D and A244N in Cas8, the A410R substitution in the helical bundle likely contacts the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex after R-loop completion (Fig. 5), potentially stabilizing the locked QCascade conformation and promoting TnsC assembly. Together, these insights suggest that evoCAST activity results from the synergistic optimization of DNA binding, intersubunit contacts, folding and solubility. Therefore, future engineering efforts should continue to use both structure-guided and directed-evolution approaches.

In conclusion, the structural findings presented here reveal the molecular mechanisms underpinning RNA-guided transposition by type I CASTs, providing a framework for their further rational engineering for technological applications.

Industry observers note that the expression plasmids containing His10–TEV-tagged TniQ and Cas8 (pSL4521), Cas7, Cas6 and the CRISPR array (pSL4522), His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsC (pSL5536) and His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsAB fusion protein (pSL3768) were cloned using standard molecular biology methods including Gibson52 and Golden Gate53 assembly. All plasmids were sequence-verified using whole-plasmid Nanopore sequencing (Genewiz). To clone the expression plasmid containing Cas7, the CRISPR array and Twin-Strep-tagged Cas6 (pMS321), a Twin-Strep-tag54 was added to the C-terminus of cas6 by Gibson assembly: pSL4522 was linearized by PCR using oMS603 and oMS604, and the Twin-Strep-tag was amplified by PCR from a common backbone using the primers oMS605 and oMS606, which contain overhangs compatible with the linearized pSL4522 plasmid. Constructs for expression of His6–MBP-tagged versions of the TnsAB fusion protein and TnsB were generated by PCR amplification of the coding sequence using pSL3768 as template and primer pairs oMS631-632 and oMS634-632, respectively. The PCR products were inserted in the 1C backbone (Addgene; 29654) by ligation-independent cloning55. The His6–MBP-tagged TnsB C-terminal tail (residues 575–613) was prepared by Gibson assembly, using the His6–MBP–TnsB plasmid as a template and the primer pairs oGF181-182 and oGF180-184 to generate the PCR fragments. Plasmids were cloned and propagated in Mach I cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), purified using the GeneJET plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and verified by full-plasmid sequencing or Sanger sequencing (Microsynth). All sequences of primers and parental plasmids used for cloning are provided in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Recent findings suggest that for Cascade–TniQ protein expression, the plasmid pSL4521 encoding His10–TEV–TniQ and Cas8 and the plasmid pMS321 encoding Cas7, Cas6–Twin-Strep and the crRNA were transformed together in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Rosetta2 (DE3) cells (Novagen), plated on an agar plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of Luria broth (LB) to obtain a starter culture. Both the transformation plate and liquid medium were supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 50 µg ml−1 streptomycin and 33 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing antibiotic-supplemented (kanamycin, streptomycin) LB medium to reach a starting optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.4 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min) and resuspended in 100 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin and 200 μg ml−1 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF). The suspension was lysed using a Maximator cell homogenizer at 1,500 bar and 4 °C. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 40 min) and applied to three 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 200 ml of HisTrap wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) and eluted with 50 ml of HisTrap elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole). Dithiothreitol (DTT) and ATP were added to the eluted sample to a final concentration of 1 mM each. The sample was added to 7 ml of 50% Strep-Tactin affinity resin suspension (IBA Lifesciences) in HisTrap elution buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 30 min. The protein-bound resin was washed with 70 ml of size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT) and the sample was eluted with 20 ml of SEC buffer supplemented with 5 mM d-desthiobiotin. Eluted fractions were further purified by SEC using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) column in SEC buffer. Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 10 mg ml−1 using a 30-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

For TnsC expression, the vector pSL5536 encoding His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was transformed in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), plated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of kanamycin-supplemented LB to obtain a starter culture. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing kanamycin-supplemented LB medium to reach a starting OD600 of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.3 mM IPTG for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min). Proteins were purified as described previously for the TnsC of Vibrio cholerae40. A cell pellet (corresponding to four 750-ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 20% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000 g at 4 °C for 45 min) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). The columns were washed with 90 ml of equilibration buffer and 50 ml of wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 30 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT), and the proteins were eluted with 10 ml of elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). Elution fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 10 mM imidazole) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Any precipitated protein was removed by centrifugation (20,000g at 4 °C for 20 min). The dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer. The columns were washed with 60 ml of equilibration buffer, 90 ml of wash buffer and 50 ml of elution buffer. Flowthrough and initial wash fractions were applied to a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 12 mg ml−1 using a 10-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

For the expression of His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsAB (pSL3768), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsAB (pMS329), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB (pMS331) and His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB(575–613) (pGF189), the procedure described for His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was followed, except that 0.4 mM IPTG was used to induce protein expression instead of 0.3 mM. For the purification of untagged TnsAB, TnsB or TnsB(575–613), a cell pellet (corresponding to four 750 ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 30% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 1 h) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 50 ml of lysis buffer, and the proteins were eluted in a stepwise gradient (5%, 20% and 100%) of elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol). Fractions corresponding to the 20% and 100% of elution-buffer concentrations were pooled and dialysed overnight in 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HiTrap Heparin HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in dialysis buffer, washed with 30 ml of dialysis buffer and eluted in a linear gradient of heparin buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) over 150 ml (target concentration of heparin buffer: 100%). Peak fractions were pooled and further purified by SEC using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 15 mg ml−1 using a 50-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use. For the expression and purification of His6–MBP-tagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), the procedures described for untagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), respectively, were followed, except that the TEV-cleavage and heparin steps were omitted.

Sources indicate that A double-stranded target DNA (dsTarget) was prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628 and oMS629 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1 ratio at a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The pull-down procedure involved mixing the assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 50 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT), 300 pmol of DNA substrate, water and 300 pmol of Cascade–TniQ and incubating this mixture at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, ATP or ATPγS (at 1 mM final concentration) was added to the sample, followed by 2,400 pmol of TnsC. The mixture was further incubated at room temperature for 30 min, after which 300 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsB(575–613) or full-length His6–MBP–TnsB was added to the sample to a final volume of 53 μl. After 30 min at room temperature, 147 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP or ATPγS) was added to the sample. Then, 10 μl were withdrawn and mixed with 10 μl of water and 5 μl of SDS dye (225 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50% (v/v) glycerol, 5% (w/v) SDS, 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 250 mM DTT) to obtain a 5% input control sample for SDS–PAGE analysis. The sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After a short centrifugation (500g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Subsequently, 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added to the sample. After centrifugation (14,000g at 4 °C for 2 min), 20 μl of supernatant was mixed with 5 μl of SDS dye to obtain an elution sample for SDS-PAGE analysis. Next, 10 μl of 5% input control and 10 μl of elution sample were loaded on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad) for each tested condition. For the control samples Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-minus or MBP–TnsB/AB-minus, the respective SEC buffers were used instead of a protein solution. SDS-PAGE gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging system (Image Lab Touch software v.4.1, Bio-Rad) and analysed using Image Lab (v.6.1.0, Bio-Rad).

In a recent development, A PseCAST pDonor plasmid was first transformed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells (NEB). Single colonies were inoculated in a liquid culture and the resulting strains were made chemically competent using standard methods. PseCAST pEffector plasmids encoding a crRNA targeting the lacZ locus (crRNA-4) and all CAST subunits were transformed in the resulting strain and plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 100 µg ml−1 spectinomycin. After approximately 20 h of growth, surviving colonies were scraped from the plates, resuspended in fresh LB medium and re-plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates supplemented with 0.1 mM IPTG to induce PseCAST protein expression. Cells were incubated for an additional 18–20 h, scraped and resuspended in LB medium. Cells were then lysed and integration efficiencies were measured using qPCR as described previously1. Data were plotted and statistical analyses performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.0, GraphPad). Wild-type plasmid sequences, crRNA-4 and oligonucleotides used for qPCR are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Recent findings suggest that the cryo-EM reconstruction of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex resulted from an initial attempt to reconstitute the QCascade–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. Target- and donor-DNA constructs were prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS572, oMS573 and oMS576 (target; Supplementary Table 3) and oMS569, oMS570 and oMS571 (donor; Supplementary Table 3) at a 1:1:1 molar ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program involved incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. For the target pot assembly, 10× buffer (200 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1,500 mM KCl, 100 mM MgCl2, 10 mM DTT), water and TniQ–Cascade were gently mixed on ice. The target DNA was added and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. TnsC and ATP were added to the sample, which was then incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The final target pot volume was 25 μl, containing 4.5 μM of Cascade–TniQ, 4.5 μM of target DNA, 40.5 μM of TnsC, 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM DTT. The donor pot was prepared by mixing 10× buffer, water, ATP, TnsAB and donor DNA to a final volume of 25 μl (containing 18 μM TnsAB, 4.5 μM of donor DNA, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT) and then incubating the mixture at room temperature for 10 min. However, a white insoluble precipitation was observed in the donor pot at this stage and again after mixing with the target pot and incubating at room temperature for 20 min. This was likely due to TnsAB instability under the conditions used. In fact, the donor pot components were not detected in the subsequent cryo-EM analysis. After mixing the target and donor pots, the sample was centrifuged (14,000g at 4 °C for 10 min) and the pellet discarded. Next, 2.5 μl of supernatant was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (30 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2 s (100% humidity, 4 °C) and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI), followed by storage in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system (University of Zurich, Switzerland) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 9,403 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 47 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 59.672 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In total, 9,403 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC56 live (v.4.3) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF (contrast transfer function) correction, 745,080 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300 Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 two-dimensional (2D) classes. Next, 416,193 particles were selected and three volumes were generated using ab initio reconstruction. One class yielded a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (108,814 particles) and was used for three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA; filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple); the other two volumes did not contain density for TnsC. Two distinct volumes, resulting from one 3DVA mode, were used as input for heterogeneous refinement to separate the particles of Cascade–TniQ–TnsC from those of Cascade–TniQ only. The two volumes, after a round of non-uniform refinement, were used as inputs for a second heterogeneous refinement, together with one of the volumes from the ab initio multi-class round. This refinement resulted in a volume of Cascade (195,798 particles), Cascade–TniQ (143,494 particles) and Cascade–TniQ–TnsC (76,901 particles). The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume was used for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction (76,400 particles), yielding a reconstruction at a resolution of 3.07 Å, as calculated by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (GSFSC). After particle subtraction, a local refinement of the TnsC heptamer generated a 3.44-Å (GSFSC resolution) map. A composite map was obtained by combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix57 (v.2.0-5936). Particles corresponding to Cascade only were used as an input for a 3DVA and heterogeneous refinement as described above. One of the resulting volumes, corresponding to 132,574 particles, yielded a 2.86-Å (GSFSC resolution) Cascade reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. The Cascade–TniQ volume was fed twice into a heterogeneous refinement. One of the volumes, corresponding to 50,074 particles, yielded a 3.19 Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. All maps and models have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 1). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. Monomeric initial models of Cas6, Cas7, Cas8, TniQ and TnsC were generated using AlphaFold3 (ref. 58). The AlphaFold3 models were docked manually as rigid bodies in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX59 (v.1.9). The model was real-space refined in Phenix (v.2.0-5936) against the cryo-EM map and then manually in Coot60 (v.0.9.4) using secondary structure, side chain rotamer, Ramachandran and LibG61 nucleic-acid restraints. The nucleic acid model, comprising the crRNA (positions −7 to 52), TGS (positions −60 to 4) and NTGS (positions −4 to 4, 21 to 23 and 34 to 60), was built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using PDB accession 7U5D (ref. 21) as a starting point. The cryo-EM density was clear enough to distinguish the DNA register. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 1. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1, Adobe). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1a–f.

According to recent reports, the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook recruitment complex was obtained using a pull-down approach. The dsTarget and a double-stranded right-end donor DNA (dsRE) were prepared by annealing synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628-629 and oMS576-630 (Supplementary Table 3), respectively, in a 1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The target pot was prepared by adding 1,200 pmol of dsTarget to 100 μl of assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT), after which KCl solution was added to a final KCl concentration of 230 mM and 1,200 pmol of Cascade–TniQ. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 10 min, after which ATP and 8,400 pmol of TnsC were added. The sample was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The final target pot volume was 200 μl and its buffer composition was 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 230 mM KCl. A donor pot was prepared by mixing 1,200 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB and 1,200 pmol of dsRE substrate. The donor pot was brought to a 20 μl final volume using TnsAB SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT), mixed with the target pot and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After adding 30 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 40 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Next, 15 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added and the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 5 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. A second elution was performed using 20 μl of maltose-supplemented binding buffer, followed by three centrifugation steps as described above. The two eluates were combined into one sample and used to freeze cryo-EM grids. Two and a half microlitres of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2.5 s at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on a FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 11,374 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.947 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

Sources indicate that in total, 11,374 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, 329,059 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300-Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 2D classes. The selected 114,608 particles were used as a training set for Topaz picking (350-Å expected particle diameter, 50 particles per micrograph), yielding 463,242 particles, which were extracted (extraction box size: 500 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 250 pixels) and classified in 150 2D classes. Classes corresponding to 189,451 particles were selected and fed into a two-class ab initio reconstruction, resulting in a junk class and a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (142,343 particles), which was used as input for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction. A 2.84-Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction was obtained from a final number of 138,834 particles, which was further used for a TnsC-focused local refinement, yielding a 2.96-Å (GSFSC resolution) volume of the heptamer decorated with additional density for each of its seven subunits. A composite map was obtained combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix (v.2.0-5936). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 2). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC model was rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The DNA duplex was extended by three nucleotides at the 5′ end of the TGS and by two nucleotides at its 3′ end, with the NTGS extended correspondingly. An initial model of the TnsC heptamer bound to seven TnsB(575–613) copies was generated using AlphaFold3 and docked manually. The model placed the last nine TnsB C-terminal residues at the additional densities of each TnsC subunit. The recognizable density of the bulky TnsB residues Trp605 and Phe612 aided in fitting the TnsB hook in the density. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 2. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1g–m.

In a recent development, the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex was prepared using a pull-down approach. The strand-transfer substrate was prepared by annealing oligos oMS733, oMS734 and oSO146 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM each. The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. Next, 1,000 pmol of substrate, 22.5 μl of assembly buffer A (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 200 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and water were mixed with 2,000 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB to a final volume of 45 μl, and the sample was kept on ice for 10 min. In the meantime, 35.8 μl (1,000 pmol) of Cascade–TniQ was mixed with 55 μl of assembly buffer B (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and 1.6 μl of water to reduce its KCl concentration to 260 mM. This mixture was added to the initial pot and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. ATP (1 mM final concentration) was added, followed by 7,000 pmol of TnsC, reaching a final volume of 155 μl. The mixture was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After the addition of 45 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1.5 h, and after centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. After adding 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose, the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. Next, 2.5 μl of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 3 s (grid 1) or 2.5 s (grid 2) at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 43,220 movies were acquired as two separate datasets (dataset 1, 11,964 movies of grid 1; dataset 2, 31,256 movies of grid 2) at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.059 e− Å−2 (dataset 1) or 65.580 e− Å−2 (dataset 2). EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In a recent development, for both datasets, the exposures were imported to cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. Datasets 1 and 2 were pre-processed separately. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, particles were identified using blob picker (270–290-Å diameter, elliptical blob), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 100 2D classes. Next, 93,462 particles of dataset 1 and 203,735 of dataset 2 were selected for a two-class ab initio reconstruction, which resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume and a TnsAB tetramer volume. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC particles were re-extracted with a bigger box size (extraction box size 1,024 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 256 pixels) and used for non-uniform refinement. Using a bigger box revealed additional density at the edge of the particles, corresponding to a flexible TnsAB tetramer next to the TnsC density. This volume was low-pass filtered and used to create masks for particle subtraction. After reducing the box size (extraction box size 700 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 350 pixels), the signal for Cascade–TniQ was subtracted from the selected set of particles and the TnsABC moiety was locally refined after aligning the volume to the centre of mass of the TnsABC mask. A 3DVA (filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple) yielded one reconstruction with clear density for both TnsC and TnsAB and another with a well-resolved TnsC density but only a weak TnsAB density. The volumes were used as input for two rounds of heterogeneous refinement with the initial set of particles. Next, 49,752 were assigned to the TnsAB-bound TnsC volume, re-extracted (576 pixels) and locally refined, focusing on TnsAB. To adjust the box size for the creation of a composite map, the particles were re-extracted with a larger box-size (700 pixels) and re-aligned to the centre of mass of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC mask, yielding a 49,606-particle set. An ab initio reconstruction, followed by non-uniform refinement, resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB consensus volume at 3.10 Å GSFSC resolution. Using the consensus map, latest masks were generated for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC, TnsC and TnsAB moieties as described above. The masks were used for particle subtraction of the TnsAB signal and local refinement of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex. To improve the signal of the TnsB hooks bound to TnsC, a final particle subtraction of the Cascade–TniQ signal was followed by local refinement of TnsC. The TnsAB local refinement was repeated using the final set of 49,606 particles to match the rest of the volumes. This procedure yielded focused cryo-EM maps for the TnsAB tetramer, the hook-bound TnsC heptamer and the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-hook complex at GSFSC resolutions of 3.36 Å, 3.30 Å and 3.09 Å, respectively. After re-alignment of the TnsAB volume, the global consensus map and the locally refined maps were combined into a composite map using the volume maximum function of ChimeraX (v.1.9). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 3). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 8. The QCascade–TnsC–TnsB hook model was rigid-body fitted in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The density corresponding to the tetrameric TnsAB was rigid-body fitted using our previously determined TnsAB PEC structure (PDB 9T7L)45. Missing regions in the protein and nucleic acid chains were built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) with the aid of an AlphaFold3 model of TnsAB. It was not possible to determine whether the hooks bound to TnsC could be assigned to any of the TnsB copies observed in the structure, as the region between the hook and the last modelled TnsB residue (TnsB(586-604)) is disordered. It should also be noted that the 7:7 TnsC:hook observed stoichiometry probably reflects the excess of bait (His6–MBP–TnsAB) used in pull-down preparations, rather than the physiological interaction ratio, which was observed to be 7:4 in other transpososome structures6,36,41. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 3. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the holocomplex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1n–r.

#142030. Breaking: Enzo Maresca is still searching for answers after Man City's draw with Napoli: There were glimpses of improvement but individual mistakes again proved their undoing, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Breaking: Enzo Maresca is still searching for answers after Man City's draw with Napoli: There were glimpses of improvement but individual mistakes again proved their undoing, writes JACK GAUGHAN

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London. Clear because there is no other appropriate message to impart, really.

He has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point. The opportunity to reignite their season, to stand up, to show the Premier League they are not going anywhere just quite yet. Squads who went before them would certainly approach a fixture of this magnitude with that attitude. A squad with Kevin De Bruyne as its linchpin would.

It has been revealed that city were still searching for answers against Napoli, a point rescued late on by Rayan Cherki. But despite the growing frustration in the stands, that unmistakable guttural desperation for just a bit more of something, it was better. More joined up thinking, at least.

According to recent reports, an inverted full back did that for them and it perhaps should be the blueprint for the manager when they arrive at the Emirates on Sunday. City were eminently more comfortable with that; knew where they stood. Nico O'Reilly was not particularly brilliant in that position yet his presence, the safety net of somebody alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi in possession and in turn freeing up Elliot Anderson will surely make City more formidable as the weeks go by.

Recent findings suggest that the set-up presented another tactical tweak for Maresca as he searches for answers and consistency. Defensively, City were twice undone by individual mistakes rather than the overarching plan, one that stifled the enduring class of De Bruyne.

A gentle hum, the half-hearted chants for a returning king, resembled an afternoon session in front of a crowd drowsy from their liquid lunches before a seesawing four-goal second half felt more befitting of City's guest for the evening, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin – intriguingly entertained by chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in the directors' box.

Rayan Cherki rescued a point late on but this was another difficult night for Man City.

Former Man United striker Rasmus Hojlund celebrates his goal against his old rivals.

Ayyoub Bouaddi scored his first goal for Manchester City since joining from Lille.

According to recent reports, city, sporting a fourth kit that had an unfortunate Guantanamo quality to it, certainly had more of a clue than they did here on Saturday. There were clearer patterns – noticeably Marc Guehi piercing midfield lines with one incisive pass for O'Reilly – but this is a team whose confidence has been shaken in recent weeks and that will not return overnight. 'We were aggressive off the ball,' stated Maresca, while bemoaning conceding for a tenth consecutive match. 'Defensively we were good, pressing good.'.

It has been revealed that regardless, City's supporters definitely demanded more caution thrown to the wind and some of their players wore those looks too. Anderson's dangerous crosses from that right-hand channel – the area presided over by De Bruyne for a decade – occasionally proved unsettling for Napoli, while Allan should have scored from a ricocheting corner as captain Erling Haaland claimed a penalty for being dragged down.

Man City (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 6; Nunes 5, Guehi 5, Gvardiol 6, O'Reilly 5; Bouaddi 7, Anderson 6; Cherki 7, Fernandez 6 (Ndiaye 63, 6), Allan 5 (Doku 54, 7); Haaland 5.

Napoli (4-1-4-1): Milinkovic-Savic 6; Spinazzola 7, Beukema 6, Rrahmani 7, Olivera 6; Gilmour 8; Politano 6, McTominay 6, De Bruyne 6, Lang 7; Hojlund 7.

Manager: Massimiliano Allegri 7.

In a sign that Maresca was placing more players in threatening areas, O'Reilly had headed over a Matheus Nunes cross – yet chances had been at a premium, those who should be protagonists taking too many safe options rather than pushing chests out and relishing responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that and when there was risk, Napoli pounced. Cherki the culprit, flicking a ball around the corner aimlessly into the middle of his own half. Billy Gilmour gave thanks, punched towards Rasmus Hojlund and he spun Guehi to flash under Donnarumma ten minutes into the second half. Hojlund celebrated by shouting 'one club in Manchester' while holding a single finger aloft. 'It's good banter,' he noted and we'll take his word for that.

City had been warned of the danger, when Noa Lang went clean through before checking back upon realising he didn't possess the acceleration to complete the job.

Maresca's assistant, Danny Walker, shook his head on the bench as they pored over the goal's replay. Enzo Fernandez was planting his boot into one of Vanja Milinkovic-Savic's posts when the goalkeeper nonchalantly plucked a floated cross from the night sky.

City had stirred somewhat though, helped by the inclusion of Jeremy Doku – ironically introduced seconds before Hojlund's opener – and it was the Belgian who made their equaliser seven minutes after the hour. He waited and waited inside Napoli's box for defenders to commit, finding Bouaddi alone and the teenager wrapped his left foot around the pass and was quickly racing back to halfway.

Sources indicate that there had appeared a head of steam, only for O'Reilly to be caught well out of position as Napoli countered – City carved open – and Lang thundered a volley past Donnarumma with 14 minutes left. Cherki made amends for his earlier error by hammering into the far corner but was less than pleased.

According to recent reports, 'We played good but we don't give a lot of energy,' Cherki remarked. 'We need to do more, we need to win these games, and today I don't care (about) scoring my goal. I want to win this game. We're going to London to win.'.

In fact, maybe that is the team talk.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

An update from training has arrived this morning, with PianetaMilan reporting that Tomori has indeed returned to training with the group at Milanello, as was hoped last night.

In fact, he has fully recovered and will be in contention for the game against Olympiacos tomorrow night, which is a major boost for Ruben Amorim, with Strahinja Pavlovic still absent.

By Matt Law | 26 Nov 2026 08:57, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 19:56.

Barcelona will continue their 2026-27 La Liga campaign against Deportivo La Coruna on Sunday afternoon.

The Catalan giants remain top of the La Liga table on 36 points, three points ahead of second-placed Real Madrid.

Here, Sports Mole rounds up all of Barcelona's injury and suspension news ahead of their contest with Deportivo, who are 12th in the division.

Espart is out for another three weeks or so due to an ankle injury; the youngster faces a battle to be unavailable before the winter break in Spain.

It has been revealed that possible return date: November 29 (vs. Deportivo).

Yamal missed out against Sabah in the Champions League on Wednesday due to a minor ankle injury, but he is expected to be fit for this match.

Bardghji was expected to leave Barcelona on loan during the summer transfer window before the news broke that he had suffered a torn ACL, which will sideline him for a significant period.

Recent findings suggest that possible return date: November 29 (vs. Deportivo).

Christensen needs to be assessed ahead of the game with Deportivo, as the centre-back has recently been on the sidelines with a calf injury.

Sources indicate that possible return date: November 29 (vs. Deportivo).

Rodri sustained a hamstring injury during the team's recent Champions League clash against Aston Villa, but he could be back on the field this weekend.

Possible return date: November 29 (vs. Deportivo).

Balde sustained an ankle injury during Barcelona's Champions League clash with Sabah on Wednesday, but he has not yet been ruled out of this match.

Recent findings suggest that possible return date: December 5 (vs. Celta Vigo).

Fermin is suspended for Barcelona's next two league matches due to the red card that he was issued in the team's league game with Villarreal last time out.

By Oliver Thomas | 26 Nov 2026 09:00.

Out-of-sorts Manchester City will be looking to end a four-match winless run in the Premier League when they lock horns with champions Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday afternoon.

The Citizens were held to a frustrating 1-1 draw at home to Fulham last weekend, which followed three league defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton & Hove Albion and Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.

Enzo Maresca's side then came from behind twice to rescue a 2-2 home draw with Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday, a game that saw Matheus Nunes recover from injury to start at right-back.

Ahead of their latest top-flight battle with Mikel Arteta's Arsenal, Sports Mole rounds up Man City’s latest injury and suspension news for this weekend's clash in North London.

Sources indicate that possible return date: December 19 (vs. Hull City).

Antonine Semenyo has been sidelined since picking up a knee injury against Ipswich Town on October 17, and the attacker is not expected to return until the middle of next month.

Man City have no suspended players for this match.

The Blues were thumped in their home cup clash with higher-division Broadbridge Heath nine days ago but responded with a 2-0 SCFL Premier win at Roffey thanks to Josh Wright’s double.

Boss Green stated: “It was a very important win. They’re up there and competing so it was similar to the East Grinstead game – it’s nice to get the wins against the teams up there with you.

"It was a cagey game, first half. First 20 minutes I thought they were the better team without really creating any chances.

"We slowly grew into the game and scored our first through Josh and we were pleased to go in 1-0 up at half-time after what was probably a 50/50 half.

"Second half I thought we went up a gear, I can’t really remember Roffey having a chance of note in the second half.

"The most notable things were three points and another clean sheet – I think it was deserved over the 90 minutes.”.
